title: Method
body:
A [[Function]] that belongs to a [[Class]]. C++ calls them *member functions*; "method" is the
word from everywhere else and the notes use both.

```c++
class IntStack {
public:
	bool push(int);      // declared inside the class
};

bool IntStack::push(int item) {    // defined with the class name
	// ...
}
```

Two things make a method different from a free function:

- **It is called on an object**: `s.push(4)`, not `push(s, 4)`. The object is implicit, and
  the method can name the private data members directly.
- **`const` after the signature** promises it does not modify the object: `bool isEmpty()
  const;`. Getters get it, setters do not.

The public methods *are* the [[Interface]]; the private data plus the method bodies are the
[[Implementation]]. That split is the point of having a class at all, see [[Encapsulation]].

Two methods with the same name and different parameters is [[Overloading]]. A subclass
replacing an inherited method is [[Overriding]]. Neither is the other.

Constructors and destructors are methods with special jobs: the constructor runs when the
object is created (`IntStack();`), the destructor when it is destroyed (`~IntStack();`), which
is where a class that allocated with `new` calls its `delete`. See [[new And delete]] and
[[Class Relationships]].
